title: Race, Disability, and Overlapping Barriers
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers

sources.title: Kimberlé Crenshaw: Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Race, Disability, and Overlapping Barriers
Examine how racial expectations, disability access, and institutional arrangements can interact in services and workplace opportunity.
Foundation self-directed learning
slides.narration: A person experiences a service as a whole, even when the organization divides its responsibilities into separate areas. Disability access, racial equity, and participation can be considered carefully in isolation while a barrier remains where the parts meet. This course introduces intersectional thinking through fictional service, workplace, and community examples. The aim is to understand interacting conditions, not rank identities or presume anyone’s experience. You will compare responses, identify what they miss, and ask what evidence could clarify the actual barrier.

slides.text:
When two good supports do not connect
An accessible English document and an inaccessible translated image are offered as separate options.

A reader needs both the translated language and screen-reader access. Neither version meets the combined need.

What would a review of each feature alone miss?
slides.narration: The team can truthfully say it supplied an accessible version and a translation. Yet the person who needs both cannot use either fully. The failure appears where the supports meet, not in the identity of the reader. Consider how the organization could describe each task as complete while missing the whole experience. Repeating that separation may leave some people consistently outside the usable route. A better inquiry checks the version a person will actually receive and leaves its effectiveness open until examined.

slides.text:
Intersectionality examines interacting power
Intersectionality asks how interacting forms of power and exclusion can disappear in a single-category explanation.

Its origins include Kimberlé Crenshaw’s examination of Black women’s experiences within race and sex discrimination frameworks.

It is more than listing identities or adding up disadvantage.
slides.narration: An intersectional question examines what an explanation leaves out when it separates conditions people experience together. Crenshaw’s foundational work matters because the concept concerns structures of power and exclusion, rather than simply having several identities. In public service, a racial assumption and a disability barrier may interact in a particular decision. That interaction must be examined, not presumed. The course uses fictional cases to make the question practical while avoiding a hierarchy of hardship or an informal identity assessment.

slides.text:
Reach the invitation and use it
A service discussion offers access support, but invitations circulate only through a familiar English-language network.

People outside that network may never reach the supported event. Repeating the route can narrow whose needs shape planning.

Examine outreach and participation together, using varied accounts.
slides.narration: An accessible meeting is valuable, but its usefulness depends partly on whether people learn about it and can respond. A familiar outreach network may reach some participants repeatedly while missing others whose experience differs. Language, race, disability, trust, and institutional connections may be relevant in different ways; none can be inferred from a name or category alone. The next case asks how to examine the whole participation route without treating separate support tasks as proof that the invitation worked.

slides.text:
Follow the whole participation route
A service discussion offers access support. Invitations circulate only through a familiar English-language network, and few perspectives reach planning. What is the best starting response?
A. Declare participation equitable because access support was offered.
B. Assume every absent racial community has the same reason for not attending.
C. Examine outreach and response routes together with varied, voluntarily offered accounts.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The support offered at the meeting is real and useful, but it answers only part of the participation question. People need to find the invitation, understand its purpose, respond, and use the activity. A familiar network may miss experiences that staff especially need to hear. Consider whether the response follows those connections or supplies a conclusion from one feature. Racial, disability, language, and institutional conditions may interact, but the case does not establish why anyone was absent. The strongest starting point combines process examination with appropriately invited perspectives.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Declare participation equitable because access support was offered.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Assume every absent racial community has the same reason for not attending.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Examine outreach and response routes together with varied, voluntarily offered accounts.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Support at the event does not establish that people reached it. Repeating a narrow invitation route can leave needs outside planning. Examine how people learn and respond; the reasons for absence remain unknown.

Which step before the meeting would you examine first, and why?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Offering support is an important action, yet attendance also depends on the route to the event. Treating that single action as proof of equity can keep a narrow invitation network unchanged. Over time, planning may reflect only people who regularly receive the opportunity. Examine the earlier steps while preserving the existing support. The case leaves absence reasons and the eventual range of participation unknown.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A group label cannot explain each absence. Repeated assumptions may lead to the wrong outreach response. Ask about routes and relevant experiences without identity profiles; language, trust, timing, and other factors are still untested.

Which step before the meeting would you examine first, and why?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Assuming one reason for a whole community converts incomplete participation information into an identity profile. Staff may then design an outreach response that misses the actual problem. Different people might encounter language, scheduling, trust, or access conditions differently. Ask relevant questions through varied channels and examine the route. A pattern could emerge, but neither a universal experience nor a single cause is supplied here.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This follows how outreach and access meet. It can reveal who is missed before support begins and inform a more usable route. Retain varied accounts and evidence limits; neither a cause nor improved participation is yet established.

Which step before the meeting would you examine first, and why?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response connects the supported activity with how people reach it. It invites knowledge that staff’s familiar network may miss without assigning any participant responsibility for a whole community. A revised route may become possible, but the inquiry must still test relevant explanations and consider feedback. It identifies a supported starting point, not a completed causal finding or guaranteed increase in participation.

slides.text:
Identity is not the problem to repair
A racial or disability identity does not explain a barrier by itself.

Ask which requirement, assumption, resource, or decision makes the activity harder to access.

Keep strengths, preferences, and agency in the account.
slides.narration: If the explanation ends with someone’s identity, the organization’s arrangements can disappear from view. A person may need a different communication format, but a document design is what makes the supplied version unusable. A racialized expectation may affect credibility, but the relevant question concerns the judgment and how it influences opportunity. Describe those conditions specifically. The person also has knowledge and preferences that can inform the response. Learning should widen their possibilities rather than reduce them to a collection of presumed disadvantages.

slides.text:
Follow where the difference is produced
Finding information, responding, being assessed, and receiving a result are connected steps.

A barrier at an early step can change who appears in later information.

Ask which point needs examination before attaching a cause to the final difference.
slides.narration: Suppose a participation summary includes only people who completed a response form. If the form was difficult to reach or use, the summary may miss people excluded before the meeting. A later difference cannot be understood only by inspecting those who arrived. Follow the relevant steps and ask where experiences diverged. Race and disability may interact with the arrangements, but an observed difference is not proof of one cause. The inquiry should identify useful evidence rather than arrive with its conclusion already attached.

slides.text:
Separate processes can leave a shared gap
One area may arrange access support while another handles outreach or response forms.

Each task can look successful while the combined route remains unusable.

State where the supports meet so the appropriate people can examine them together.
slides.narration: Specialization brings useful expertise, and intersectional thinking does not require one person to take over every role. It asks whether the separate arrangements connect in the experience people actually have. An accessible invitation leading to an inaccessible registration form illustrates the gap. Staff can describe that connection clearly and seek an appropriate joint review. Merely recording that each area completed its assigned task may reproduce the barrier. The relevant outcome is a usable route, which still requires evidence beyond the coordination conversation.

slides.text:
Do not turn complexity into a ranking
No identity inventory can calculate a person’s hardship or predict their choices.

A person can encounter a barrier in one setting and have an advantage in another.

Ask about the task and necessary information without demanding a personal biography.
slides.narration: Complexity is not a reason to rank people by the number of identities they disclose. Such a ranking would invite stereotypes without explaining which arrangement needs attention. A person’s experience can vary across activities and over time. Begin with the opportunity they are trying to access and the information appropriate to that question. Actual eligibility or accommodation processes retain their own requirements and responsible roles. A voluntary learning exercise should not imitate those processes or gather unnecessary sensitive information.

slides.text:
Access to training is not access to opportunity
An employee can use the training room, yet project leads choose mentees through a familiar informal network.

Racial expectations and inaccessible networking arrangements may interact in who receives development opportunities.

Examine the criteria, invitation routes, and employee’s account before deciding why.
slides.narration: A usable training room addresses one important condition. It does not explain how people gain the relationships or assignments through which learning becomes advancement. In this fictional example, the informal route matters because it influences mentoring. Racial assumptions, disability access, scheduling, or other conditions could shape that route differently. Those possibilities need evidence. The next choice asks how to investigate without declaring training access sufficient or assuming the employee’s identity explains the outcome.

slides.text:
Training access and mentoring access
An employee can use the training room but does not reach informal mentoring opportunities. Racial expectations and inaccessible networking may be relevant. What response best examines the concern?
A. Inspect opportunity criteria, invitation routes, and the employee’s chosen account together.
B. Conclude that physical room access proves equal development opportunity.
C. Attribute the outcome to the employee’s identities without examining the process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The employee’s experience points to two different aspects of development. Using the room makes formal training possible. Reaching mentoring opportunities may depend on invitations, relationships, scheduling, or judgments about potential. Race and disability can matter through those conditions, but their relevance must be examined in context. Consider which response investigates the connected opportunity and which treats a single feature or identity as the answer. No personal biography is needed for this exercise, and the fictional case does not establish a discriminatory finding or the employee’s preferred arrangement.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Inspect opportunity criteria, invitation routes, and the employee’s chosen account together.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Conclude that physical room access proves equal development opportunity.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Attribute the outcome to the employee’s identities without examining the process.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This examines how the supports and opportunity route interact. It may reveal a repeated gate between training and development. Ask what evidence supports each explanation; the cause and preferred support remain unknown.

What could a training-access review miss about later development?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Inspecting the actual route connects access with how development opportunities are distributed. The employee can offer relevant knowledge without being required to disclose everything about their life. If a repeated invitation habit favors only familiar participants, that may help explain the gap. Other explanations may also matter. The inquiry should retain what is supported and leave cause, motive, and the effect of any proposed change open.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Room access does not explain mentoring decisions. Repeating this conclusion may leave an informal opportunity gate untouched. Examine criteria and routes alongside access; equal development opportunity is not established.

What could a training-access review miss about later development?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: An accessible room addresses an important barrier but cannot establish how mentees are chosen. Treating it as sufficient may preserve a network that limits who receives opportunities after training. Ask what criteria and invitation channels operate and whether people can use them. The evidence establishes room access in this example; it does not establish comparable mentoring access or a cause of the employee’s experience.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Identity is not the process to repair. Repeating this inference can profile employees and miss changeable conditions. Examine the actual decisions and listen appropriately; motive, cause, and the wider pattern are unknown.

What could a training-access review miss about later development?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Attributing the outcome directly to identities can obscure the institutional choices that could be examined. It may also make the employee a subject of profiling instead of a partner in understanding opportunity. Describe the mentoring route, relevant access conditions, and criteria. The employee’s account may clarify an interaction, but the case does not establish an automatic identity effect or the wider distribution of opportunities.

slides.text:
Look across relevant life-cycle decisions
Recruitment, onboarding, assignments, development, and advancement may use different routes to opportunity.

An early access barrier or credibility judgment can influence a later decision.

Trace the connection that matters; do not assume every stage works the same way.
slides.narration: An employee life-cycle view helps locate where a specific opportunity becomes available or restricted. For example, an onboarding introduction may affect who learns about a project, and a project assignment may later count as experience for advancement. That is a possible pathway, not proof that each stage is unequal. Examine the actual criteria and route. Different roles and stages may require different questions. A useful review follows the connection supported by evidence rather than forcing one explanation across every employment decision.

slides.text:
A group difference is a question, not a verdict
A difference in outcomes can justify careful inquiry without establishing its cause.

Ask who is included, what the denominator describes, and whether information is comparable.

Small or incomplete categories may conceal variation and uncertainty.
slides.narration: A percentage means little without knowing which population it describes. A rate among applicants differs from a rate among all people who might need a service. If barriers affect who applies, focusing only on applicants can miss part of the question. Small numbers and inconsistent information also limit interpretation. Do not dismiss the difference or treat it as proof of a chosen explanation. State what the information can show and which process evidence or lived experience could deepen understanding.

slides.text:
Prepare with briefs, then hear varied experience
Community briefs can introduce history, institutions, and relevant questions.

They cannot establish how race and disability combine for a particular person.

Invite perspectives that do not fit a single category, without requiring disclosure or representation.
slides.narration: A brief may alert you to histories or institutional relationships relevant to participation. The individual still holds knowledge about their own experience that the document cannot provide. Seek varied accounts through appropriate, usable routes and make their scope clear. People should not need to disclose a diagnosis or speak for an entire racial community to offer useful feedback. When staff repeatedly consult only familiar representatives, combinations of experience outside those networks may remain invisible. Preparation should widen inquiry, not supply the answer.

slides.text:
Test whether the supports work together
Consider the actual document, invitation, response route, and activity a person will use.

Improving one feature may leave another barrier intact.

A joined-up proposal is a useful beginning; effectiveness still needs appropriate checks and feedback.
slides.narration: A response should be examined at the point where the original difficulty appeared. Translating a document does not solve access if the final file remains unreadable to the technology the person uses. Offering access support at an event does not solve an invitation gap. Ask whether the combination now works in the actual sequence, with appropriate review and voluntary feedback. Be specific about what improved and what did not. A partial change may be valuable without being described as complete access for everyone.

slides.text:
An accessible invitation leads to a closed route
A community invitation is translated and accessible. Its registration form requires English, and access requests are available only after registration.

The sequence can exclude people before support is arranged.

Examine the whole route and ask which alternatives would be usable.
slides.narration: The initial invitation looks inclusive when reviewed alone. The response form and timing of support create a different experience. A person who cannot use registration may never reach the stage where access is offered. If repeated, the sequence could leave some combinations of need systematically outside participation. The next choice asks which response addresses this connection. No participant’s preferences, legal conclusion, or complete community pattern is supplied; the fiction identifies a route that deserves examination.

slides.text:
Supports separated by the registration step
An accessible translated invitation leads to an English-only registration form. Access requests become available only after registration. Which response best addresses the connected barrier?
A. Provide more copies of the same invitation.
B. Review registration and support timing together, seeking usable alternatives and appropriate feedback.
C. Mark translation and access complete because each exists somewhere in the process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The invitation has two useful features, yet the next step prevents some people from reaching the support offered later. The sequence is the central issue. Consider whether a response changes that connection or simply adds more of what already exists. A usable alternative should be examined through the appropriate responsibilities and informed by people’s varied experiences. A community brief can prepare relevant questions, but it cannot tell you what every participant needs. The fiction supplies a potential barrier in the route, not a completed legal finding or a tested solution.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Provide more copies of the same invitation.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Review registration and support timing together, seeking usable alternatives and appropriate feedback.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Mark translation and access complete because each exists somewhere in the process.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
More invitations do not change the response barrier. Repeating the sequence may exclude people before support is offered. Examine registration and access timing; the usable alternative and actual participation effects are unknown.

How would you check the route a participant actually receives?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Distributing more of the invitation may broaden awareness while leaving the same form and timing unchanged. People who cannot complete that step still cannot request support. If sustained, the sequence may repeatedly filter participation before the organization recognizes the need. Examine the response route and consider an appropriate alternative. The case does not establish which alternative works or whether more distribution changes anyone’s experience.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This addresses the point where separate supports fail to connect. It may reduce exclusion before registration is complete. Check the actual revised route and hear relevant accounts; a proposal alone does not prove access.

How would you check the route a participant actually receives?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response focuses on the interaction rather than blaming a person or discarding useful supports. Registration and access timing can be considered together so a need is not recognized only after the person passes an unusable gate. The revised route still requires appropriate checks and voluntary feedback. It is a supported proposal, with practical effectiveness and the range of participation remaining open.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Separate completed tasks can conceal an unusable whole. Repeating this check can keep some needs outside participation. Test how the features work together; completion labels do not establish the person’s experience.

How would you check the route a participant actually receives?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The completion labels describe separate tasks, not whether the participant can move through the process. Accepting those labels as the outcome may reproduce the same gap each time the invitation is used. Examine the actual version and sequence people receive, retaining existing useful features. The supplied facts show that supports exist separately; they do not show that combined participation needs are met.

slides.text:
Distinguish explanation from accusation
You can identify a possible barrier without deciding anyone’s complete motive.

Describe the action, its plausible effect, and the evidence that would test the connection.

Clear questions make a concern easier to examine without weakening its importance.
slides.narration: A question about a familiar-network invitation does not require a claim that everyone involved intended exclusion. It asks whether the route shapes whose knowledge becomes visible. Intent and effect can both matter, but they need different evidence. Describe the mechanism in terms another person can inspect: how the opportunity is announced, what response is required, and who can use it. This specificity avoids blanket accusations while retaining the serious equity question. The explanation should remain open to information that changes it.

slides.text:
Keep the person’s whole experience visible
One office’s completed task is not the same as a person’s usable experience.

Listen for where transitions between supports create difficulty.

Preserve the person’s chosen priorities rather than deciding that staff coordination is their main goal.
slides.narration: People may value a timely decision, understandable information, a chosen support relationship, or the ability to contribute. Organizational coordination is useful when it helps those goals; it is not itself the person’s desired outcome. Ask where the current route falls short and what matters most in the situation. Avoid making the person repeatedly explain the same concern to every area. A clearer connection between responsibilities may reduce that burden, but its effect still needs information from the actual experience.

slides.text:
Rewrite a single-category explanation
Take the fictional training or registration case.

Write what a disability-only or race-only account might notice and miss.

Then describe an interacting condition, a better question, and one limit of the evidence.
slides.narration: The purpose of this reflection is to make your reasoning visible. In the training case, a room-access account may miss the mentoring route. A racial-equity account may overlook whether the networking activity itself is usable. Describe the relevant connection without assuming the same experience for every employee. Then write a question that could clarify the mechanism. Your reflection can remain private and use only the fiction. An honest limit does not erase the concern; it identifies what the next inquiry needs.

slides.text:
Compare a change with the original barrier
Ask whether the proposed response addresses the connection that caused difficulty.

Consider whether the change shifts a burden to another step or another group.

Retain missing information rather than treating silence as success.
slides.narration: A change can solve one problem while introducing another. A new response route might be accessible but available only during hours some people cannot use. Compare the revised sequence with the original concern and seek relevant feedback through appropriate channels. Do not assume that no complaint means everyone could participate. You may know what staff changed while remaining uncertain about the range of effects. That distinction makes follow-through more useful and avoids claiming that an incomplete review settled a wider disparity.

slides.text:
Ask about the interaction that matters
Intersectional thinking examines conditions and power people experience together.

Keep identity, agency, evidence, and uncertainty distinct.

Continue with accessibility, racial equity, community engagement, and data resources as the question requires.
slides.narration: You have practiced moving from separate categories toward a specific interaction in a service or opportunity. The strongest question concerns what the current explanation misses, not how many identities a person has. Race and disability remain important without becoming automatic causes or a ranking of hardship. Follow the experience, hear varied perspectives, and examine supports where they meet. A response can address a plausible barrier while leaving broader findings open. Continued learning should deepen that inquiry rather than replace it with a label.

outcomes: Explain intersectionality through interacting conditions rather than a list or ranking of identities.
Identify how separate support processes may miss a combined barrier.
Ask what information could clarify a difference in experience without assuming its cause.
Consider an improvement that addresses access and racial equity together.
